parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
In computed tomography (CT scanning), it is necessary to take a series of many X-ray images.
Outline briefly the principles of CT scanning.

markscheme_points.text: images (of one slice) taken from different
to build up 3D image (of whole body/struct

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking small. A normal X-ray shows everything overlapped, so what thin piece of the body does a CT machine focus on at one time?
Hint 2: Think about movement. If you want 3D information from 2D shadows, why would you need to rotate the X-ray tube and detectors around the patient?
Hint 3: Think about the computer's job. How are all those different directional views of the same slice combined?
Hint 4: Think about building up. Once you have one slice imaged clearly, how do you get the whole organ or body?
parts.proper_answer: X-rays image one thin slice/section at a time. Many images of that same slice are taken from different angles around the body. A computer processes these to form a 2D image of the slice. This is repeated for many slices to build up a 3D image of the structure.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Think in Slices, Not Shadows**
Imagine a loaf of bread. A normal X-ray is like looking through the whole loaf at once, so everything overlaps. CT is different. You isolate just one thin slice through the body at a time. That is why many images are needed.

Step 2: **Look From All Around**
For that one slice, the X-ray tube rotates around the patient. It fires a narrow beam through the slice and detectors on the opposite side measure how much is transmitted. This is repeated from many different directions, typically through 360 degrees. Different tissues attenuate X-rays differently, so each direction gives different information about the same voxels.

Step 3: **Let the Computer Reconstruct**
A computer takes all those directional attenuation readings for the one slice and works backwards to find the attenuation of each small voxel. It then displays this as a 2D grey-scale image of that slice, showing soft tissue detail that a plain X-ray cannot.

Step 4: **Stack Slices Into 3D**
The tube then moves along slightly and the whole process is repeated for the next slice. By stacking many 2D slice images together, the computer builds up a full 3D image of the organ or body that can be rotated and viewed from any angle.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A student creates a model for CT scanning.
A section is divided into four voxels, with pixel numbers $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$, as shown in Fig. 9.1.
{{figure:figure_9_1}}
Fig. 9.1
The section is viewed from four different directions $V_1$, $V_2$, $V_3$ and $V_4$, as shown in Fig. 9.1.
The detector readings for each direction are noted and then summed. The result is shown in Fig. 9.2.
{{figure:figure_9_2}}
Fig. 9.2
The background count is 26.
Determine the pixel numbers $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ as shown in Fig. 9.1.
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 9.2 and the background count of 26. The numbers 47, 59, 44, 32 are too large because they include unwanted counts present in every measurement. What must you remove first?

Hint 2: After removing the background, each voxel has been counted more than once because it was seen in several of the views V1 to V4. The model tells you the true pixel value is shared equally - what division gives the values in the mark scheme?
Hint 3: Now apply the two operations in order to each position: top-left for A, top-right for B, bottom-left for D, bottom-right for C, and check that all four give whole numbers.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Understand the Summed Image**
In this simple model each square in Fig. 9.2 is the sum of the readings that passed through that voxel from the different directions. So it contains the real pixel value added several times plus the background count that is present even with no absorption difference. You cannot just read A as 47.

Step 2: **Subtract the Background**
First remove the part that is common to everything and carries no image information:
$$ \text{signal} = \text{summed reading} - \text{background} $$
With background $= 26$:
$$ 47-26 = 21, \quad 59-26 = 33, \quad 44-26 = 18, \quad 32-26 = 6 $$

Step 3: **Divide to Get the True Pixel**
In this 4-view model each true voxel value has been added 3 times in the summation process. So to recover the single voxel value:
$$ \text{pixel number} = \frac{\text{summed reading} - 26}{3} $$
$$ A = \frac{21}{3} = 7, \quad B = \frac{33}{3} = 11 $$
$$ D = \frac{18}{3} = 6, \quad C = \frac{6}{3} = 2 $$
That gives $A = 7$, $B = 11$, $D = 6$, $C = 2$, matching the layout in Fig. 9.1.
